scenes.heading: Partition Pruning
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Partition Pruning and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What pruning saves
items: Skips reading partitions that can't match a filter
Cuts I/O dramatically on large tables
scenes.narration: Partition pruning lets Spark skip entire chunks of data that cannot possibly satisfy a query's filter. It works when a table is physically partitioned into directories by column values, such as a date. By reading only the relevant directories, pruning can turn a full-table scan into a tiny targeted read.

scenes.heading: How pruning is applied
scenes.narration: When data is written partitioned by a column, Spark stores each value in its own directory. If your query filters on that same column, Catalyst matches the predicate against the directory structure and drops every partition that cannot match. Only the surviving files are handed to the scan, so unmatched data is never opened.

scenes.code:
# Written partitioned by event_date
df.write.partitionBy("event_date").parquet("/data/events")

# This read prunes to a single day's directory
day = (spark.read.parquet("/data/events")
          .filter("event_date = '2026-07-01'"))
day.explain()  # PartitionFilters shows the pruning
scenes.heading: Static partition pruning
scenes.narration: The write lays out data into one directory per event_date value. When the read filters on event_date, Spark scans only that one day's directory instead of the whole dataset. The explain output confirms this under PartitionFilters, distinct from the DataFilters applied to non-partition columns. Choosing a good partition column is what makes this optimization possible.

scenes.heading: Static vs dynamic pruning
scenes.narration: Static pruning happens when the filter is a constant known at planning time. Dynamic partition pruning goes further: when a fact table joins a small dimension table, Spark derives the partition filter from the dimension at runtime and prunes the fact scan accordingly. This is especially powerful in star-schema warehouses where the pruning key only becomes known after the join.

scenes.text: Partition on columns you filter by, but avoid tiny over-partitioning.
scenes.narration: The best partition column is one you query on often and that yields reasonably sized files. Too many small partitions reintroduces the small-files problem.
